Our analytical calculations reveal the coexistence of phases with different parity and Chiral symmetry breaking, and these results agree with previous numerical simulations. Furthermore, we extended the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ invariant theory to the case of a general magnetic field and found that the phase boundaries change smoothly when the flux increases. We also identified additional phases that occur due to orbital mixing. In the regime of strong magnetic field, the phase diagram of three-dimensional Weyl metal reduces to the known cases, and our theory can be extended to other systems that are topological by the time-reversal symmetry breaking effect.

The development of highly efficient, coherent light sources with controlled radiation patterns is crucial for advancing quantum information processing, cavity quantum electrodynamics, and studies on two-photon processes. We propose a novel approach to achieve these goals, capitalizing on the hybridization of electric and magnetic resonances in 3D nanoantenna designs. By combining a dielectric (Si) and a plasmonic (Ag/Au) material in a specific geometry, we create an antenna that exhibits exceptional performance characteristics, including high Unidirectional and luminous factors. When employed as part of a single-photon source, this antenna demonstrates enhanced brightness and anti-bunching performance compared to conventional emitters and a reference dielectric antenna. We experimentally validate the theoretical model by creating Si (400 nm) - Au (80 nm) nanostructures using electron beam lithography and measuring their two-photon radiation patterns using multicolor imaging of in situ two-photon coincidences. Our findings reveal excellent agreement between experimental results and the theoretical predictions. We believe that this study provides valuable insights for designing and optimizing nanoantenna structures for the development of highly efficient, unidirectional, and coherent light sources.

Monolayer granular sheets exhibit a unique screening property, reducing force carriers over long-range potential, yet the underlying mechanics of this phenomenon remain poorly understood. Recent research suggested that a non-standard screening model, involving spatially varying potentials, could effectively describe this phenomenon, but validation in real-time was missing. Our study combines experimental and numerical methods to support the idea that the standard screening model is inadequate and the anomalous one is necessary to accurately describe granular materials. By introducing a non-Newtonian model of electric conductivity that reflects the dynamic interactions within granular sheets, we were able to produce empirical and simulation results that converged, validating the anomalous screening model.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research focuses on the electronic properties of manganese-decorated silicene, which is placed on a hexagonal boron nitride surface. By integrating a 1T silicene layer with a BNN monolayer, we examine the influence of vertical separation distances and binding energies. Our analysis reveals that the interaction between the Orbetello-Arno model and BNN monolayer, which has a binding energy of approximately 2.06 eV, produces the best outcomes. Within this configuration, our density-of-states results show that the manganese atom shifts the Fermi level up by 0.434 eV, while displaying distinct resonant bands. Moreover, our study demonstrates the ability to tune the electrical properties of manganese-decorated silicene using vertical separation distances and binding energies.

The Sgr A East radio filament is a long, sinuous emission feature, thought by some to be a 10,000-20,000 year old expansion shock from a supernova, and by others, the remains of a cloud compressed by the O-star cluster $\omega$ Centauri at the centre of the galaxy. Recent findings from ALMA and VLA observations suggest the filament is part of a much larger, 40-80 $\mu$Jy structure, with multiple emission shocks. A new model has been proposed that accommodates these new data, proposing the supernova originated from a star that weighed around 20-40 solar masses, near the center of the galaxy, and around 150-200 parsecs from the event's centre. A nearby molecular cloud was compressed by the shock from this supernova, creating the Sgr A East bubble and its characteristic emission shocks. This new model further proposes the Sgr A East bubble and its associated radiation, was formed around 6-17 parsec from the event's centre, and that the Sgr A East bubble and its associated radiation, was formed around 6-17 parsec from the event's centre, and that the Sgr A East bubble and its radiation, was formed around 6-17 parsec from the event's centre, and that the Sgr A East bubble and its radiation, was formed around 6-17 parsec from the event's centre, and that the Sgr A

Overcoming class imbalance issues in NLP poses a significant challenge, and a effective technique to address this problem is oversampling. A novel, efficient, and easy-to-implement oversampling method called Frame was recently proposed, built on the concept of frame algebras. This method offers a versatile framework that allows for customizing the creation of new class instances. In this study, Frame is tested alongside three other state-of-the-art oversampling methods: Safe Aggregate, Safe Bonding, and Borderline. The evaluation involves the Multi-genre Text Opinion Sources dataset, and four different oversampling configurations of Frame are explored. The analysis examines data distribution changes resulting from oversampling in specific subgroups. The study also introduces a new quantitative measure to assess class distribution diversity. The performance of the oversampling methods is evaluated using multi-class precision, recall, and F1 scores. Experimentation reveals that Frame achieves the most substantial improvement in target minority class recall while maintaining overall macro F1 score compared to the other evaluated oversampling techniques.

This study analyzes data from an online local news database, combining news articles from 2020 to 2021 with COVID-19 case and death data in the United States. It examines the link between local news coverage, COVID-19 outcomes, and audience characteristics. Findings indicate that areas with more stringent mitigation measures and higher infection rates received greater news coverage. News volume exhibited an inverse relationship with local population size. COVID-related stories comprised nearly 1 in 10 total news items and nearly 1 in 5 health-related news items. Such stories appeared more frequently in areas with higher infection rates and death counts. These stories were relatively rare in newspapers with lower circulation numbers. In response to rising cases in June 2021, news coverage increased. This surge was more pronounced in areas with higher infection rates. Slightly over 1 in 10 readers engaged with COVID-related news through comments or other interactive features. Such engagement rose in areas with higher infection rates and decreased in areas with lower circulation.

Implementing the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) in parallel requires careful management to prevent unbalanced workload distribution and incorrect data transmission. This study focuses on optimizing FMM for sparse matrix-vector multiplication, specifically addressing preservation of angular momentum in the translation matrix representation. By incorporating this principle, the challenge of maintaining angular momentum during FMM evaluations is addressed. A comprehensive analysis of FMM is provided, including the identification of sources contributing to angular momentum violation. Furthermore, a theoretical expression for total angular momentum is derived and practical guidelines for achieving accurate results are outlined. A high-level description of FMM implementation is also presented, incorporating the use of task queues and tree structures, as well as a method for detecting parallel team synchronization issues.

Numerical calculations exploring the proton's polarization transfer in the specific reaction $e \vec {p} \to e \vec {p}$ have been conducted for various energy and momentum cut-off criteria. Notably, when considering a square momentum transfer scale of $Q^2$ less than 1 GeV$^2$, approximately 80% of the time, the final proton's polarization will be polarized in the same direction as the initial one's; this occurs for kinematic conditions resulting from charged-current lepton scattering on polarized targets where a large majority of events feature the lepton-nucleon scattering vector making an angle of less than $\pi/4$ radians with the nucleon's spin axis.

In a scenario where multiple experienced, parametric models are available but not fully trusted, it's possible to develop a powerful, combined model by integrating their predictions. This process, known as ensemble learning or information fusion, or potentially maximum likelihood learning, has numerous practical applications in fields, including machine learning-based navigation and control, where models are often viewed as sources of probabilistic information rather than pure prediction tools. This study focuses on the issue of enhancing data to learn from these models. It's hypothesized that, in most cases, the best method is to create synthetic samples by combining the expected mean and variance from each model, making this approach simple to implement, efficient, and effective. This hypothesis was supported through experiments on two critical issues: model combination and pretraining. Further tests showed that even small amounts of untrusted data can improve the performance of deep neural networks when trained using synthetic data generated through this method, often as effectively as using much larger amounts of trusted data.

A study investigating the non-production of Higgs boson pairs (HH) alongside a vector boson (V) in high-energy proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider is reported. The LHC's sensor, the ATLAS detector, was utilized in 2015-2016 to collect 36.1 fb^-1 of data. The research explores the phenomena $\mathrm{t\overline{t}}$ + H and $\mathrm{b\overline{b}}$ + H + V, as well as other associated HHV productions, and sets bounds on their respective cross-sections relative to the corresponding standard model processes. The investigation further includes two-channel non-resonant HH productions: HHq¯q¯ and HHgg, and provides the most stringent constraints on these processes to date. The research assumes the 125 GeV Higgs boson was produced.

We've developed an innovative approach to creating extremely coherent light with a new type of laser. By using an ultra-cold rubidium atom cloud as the gain medium and developing a novel electronic control system, we were able to produce 30 milliwatts of light with an exceptionally low level of noise. This breakthrough is due in large part to the cloud's natural instability, which is counteracted by an innovative digital feedback loop. The loop rapidly adjusts to maintain the perfect balance of population inversion, resulting in a highly coherent state. A new compact design, combined with the advanced digital control, has allowed us to achieve this level of coherence in a setting where more traditional methods fall short.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, we establish a lower bound for the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant at the identity element of the associated algebraic torus component, based on the dimension 'r' of the Siegel disk and the maximum 'b' of the Jacobian. This bound proves to be sufficiently large when the dimension 'r' equals 1. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the upper bound for the logarithmic height of 'b' tends towards infinity as the parameter 'r' increases. This investigation originates from a previous study on the dynamics of iterated function systems, which also yielded significant results across all compact moduli spaces of K3 surfaces.

In the context of supersymmetry, a decaying neutralino as dark matter is investigated, with the possibility that it decays into either the scalar Higgs boson or a gauge boson. Since dark matter is self-interacting and has a mass greater than approximately 93 GeV, it does not contradict recent experiments including those from the LHC and dark matter direct detection studies. With a mass less than the Higgs boson, decays into the Higgs boson and gamma rays via bremsstrahlung and internal bremsstrahlung processes are feasible. If its mass exceeds the Higgs boson mass, decays into a gauge boson and gamma rays become possible. With a mass less than 93 GeV, decays into gauge bosons are only feasible below a certain threshold velocity due to the relativistic nature of dark matter. The research explores internal bremsstrahlung and bremsstrahlung processes in a narrow line and continuous spectrum, and discusses detectability using gamma ray telescopes such as Fermi and future advanced telescopes with greater sensitivity.

The main objective of this research is to develop an efficient method for approximating the minimum genus $\min g(H)$ of a dense graph $H$, given a specified target $0 < \varepsilon < 1$. By applying the Heawood inequality and dividing the graph into subgraphs of specified sizes, an innovative algorithm is presented. This algorithm enables the computation of an estimate for the minimum genus within a specified range in polynomial time. This approach is grounded in Sanita's recent discovery. A comprehensive explanation of the former's implications is provided, offering a more refined understanding of previous methods, including those developed by Grant and Wilson (1991) and Thomassen (1989). Additionally, our technique enables the creation of an efficient $O(n)$-time algorithm for finding a surface where the given graph $H$ can be embedded with a minimum genus not exceeding a specified bound. This method can also approximate the minimum genus within a specified range in sublinear time.

A persistent challenge in network optimization is the need for individual nodes to collaborate and share information with a central node, although this can lead to congestion and inefficiency. To address this, we develop a novel algorithm combining Newton's method with stochastic rounding, which allows individual nodes to make local calculations while periodically sending updated gradient vectors to a central node for updating the collective optimal solution. We show through theoretical analysis and practical tests that this algorithm can achieve faster convergence rates, require fewer communication rounds, and be more resilient in the presence of noise compared to traditional methods.

Social media platforms have seen the emergence of toxic and hateful content driven by significant global events such as the migration and COVID-19 crises, which critical experts believe pose a serious threat to society's well-being. In the face of this danger, scientists and engineers are uniting to develop advanced technologies capable of detecting and combating hate speech in online platforms. Previous studies have primarily focused on English language data, neglecting the vast pool of resource-poor languages spoken by significant portions of the world's population. This research seeks to bridge this gap by analyzing the effectiveness of hate speech detection techniques on Hindi and Bengali datasets and leveraging transfer learning to aid in the identification of toxic content. Using X-MOCAP and HMPOC Hindi and Bengali datasets, we trained and tested neural network models such as CNN, CharCNN, LSTMs, and Attention-based models. Our findings show that the Hindi language achieved higher hate speech detection accuracy compared to Bengali, with the Convolutional Neural Network delivering superior performance across both languages. Additionally, our experiments demonstrated the applicability of transfer learning in the context of our task.

In particle detectors with gas time projections, the electron drift field usually
triggers the primary signal, yet its information is compromised due to the drone
movement resulting from electron-ion pairs separation. This drone's presence
affects point resolution, leading some devices to disable the drift field. Although
drift field offers benefits like ion feedback, recharge time, and charge neutrality,
some detectors have given it up. We present here some alternative signals derived
from the drift field with the intention of overcoming the drone's detrimental impact.
These signals can remain active throughout the detection process, providing the
detector with improved sensitivity and operation efficiency. Moreover, these
signals are not influenced by ion feedback and are detectable even in cases of ion
recoil, thus enabling the detection of such events. As a result, these signals are not
only beneficial for general detectors, but they are particularly essential for dark
matter searches where recoil events are a crucial aspect of the experiment.

In various industries such as transportation, self-driving cars and commercial trucks are now equipped with black-box algorithms making crucial safety-critical decisions, yet these systems lack transparency. Unlike human judgment, these algorithms are not capable of taking context into consideration, for example, road conditions, to make informed decisions. The outcome is that drivers and operators may lose confidence in the capability of these vehicles to make informed spatial planning choices. To address this concern, we set up a user-centered design that involves an expert review of the decisions made by these algorithms. The partnership involves asking experts from the logistics and transportation field whether the self-driving car would stop at an intersection it has identified, and if so where it would stop. The decision to stop would be based on visual inputs such as traffic signals and road signs at that particular location. The integration of these algorithms and expert feedback enables self-driving cars to make more informed spatial planning choices, ultimately leading to greater success in achieving set goals such as arriving on schedule at a destination. We tested the performance of these vehicles by comparing their ability to achieve set goals with and without using the decision-making capabilities of these algorithms, and found a significant 21\% improvement.

The Out-of-Category challenge held at the PAKDD 2021 conference pushed the limits of deep learning methods for multiclass classification in data science by introducing a novel representation of outside categories. This challenge forced models to make a distinction between known class labels and unknown ones. A series of theoretical models were proposed that proved an increased error rate is needed for identifying extra categories when using a limited feature set derived from the target variables. To verify these findings, a series of experiments were conducted on datasets commonly used in multiclass classification within the data science community. A comprehensive evaluation was carried out on seven datasets that revealed an significant increase in error rates for features extracted from target variables compared to within-category errors. Furthermore, proposed error increment models showed a strong predictive performance with a relatively low number of parameters compared to baseline models, with an approximately 10-fold lower parameter count. A comparative analysis across various deep learning optimizers revealed RMSprop to be the most effective choice for optimizing model weights, resulting in an average 21.9% reduction in error rates. Our code and implementation for within-category and out-of-category errors can be found at the link below: https://github.com/M-M-M/f1-score-and-cross-entropy.

Random fluctuations in the early universe can form diverse patterns, 
which can be mathematically represented as a Gaussian field manifold. 
This pattern formation is similar to geodesic lines on these manifolds. 
Unlike usual calculations which involve approximations based on specific patterns, 
our method directly generates geometric patterns from the underlying probability distribution. 
This approach has been developed and demonstrated on a two-dimensional plane, 
which shows that geometric patterns generated from different probability distributions 
are distinct and follow a simple equation. 
Moreover, our geodesic patterns conserve symmetry and show correlation with the underlying probability distribution. 
This method can be applied to various Gaussian field manifolds and has been used to 
investigate complex patterns in a model of the universe and those formed by 
interfering waves in chaotic systems.

Revised Reuter comb model. Reuter's 1963 length spectrum criterion for planar linkages is reinterpreted using a modified model. This criterion can be translated into a simple maximum modulus problem, solved through a straightforward application of Bezier methods. Within a specific parameter interval, the solution evolves periodically. A notable outcome arises when the parameter approaches infinity, providing an insightful regrouping of Reuter's conditions. A practical demonstration of this model is offered: designing a planar linkage that constructs a regular hexagon with a specified side length. A supplemental video further illustrates the solution's periodic nature.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ of weight greater than $1/2$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, the least common multiple of the absolute values of $L(F,\chi,n)$, where $L(F,\chi,n)$ is the $n$th Vandiver criterion value, serves as an bounds on a key component of the $n$th stage of the modular form's critical period under the Ramanujan-Vinogradov conjecture, or else it is simply the product of the $L$-functions' zeros and the 1 if $\chi$ is the trivial character.

In experimental settings, graphene properties can be modified to meet specific needs by converting it into nanoribbons. Research has shown through computational models that these nanorbons exhibit unique electrical characteristics. A study focusing on armchair graphene nanoribbons found that an applied gate voltage allows for precise control over spin-dependent transport properties. A non-zero magnetic field affects the energy states of spin-up and spin-down electrons equally, yet the energy states of spin-up electrons in ring-shaped graphene structures exhibit distinct differences from those of spin-down electrons.

We derive approximation theorems for operators with weak nonlinearity and monotonicity properties, applicable for any Banach space with a differenceable unit ball. We establish theorems for convolution-type operators acting on Banach spaces with certain regularity properties. Additionally, we provide convergence results for approximating operators in the graph norm of the difference. Our results include convergence in the quasi-Banach case, exemplified by operators with Lipschitz boundary conditions on the unit ball.

A subset of vertices in a graph is called a pancyclic set if it allows a cycle of every possible length to be formed. A notable result states that if a graph has an independent subset equal to at least c4n, where c is a constant, it must also be a pancyclic graph. This result was originally proven by Chvatal in 1972. Now, a new result has shown that we can decrease the independence count to approximately c0.16 n to arrive at the same conclusion. Additionally, it has been shown that we can replace the independence subset with a subset of hamiltonian cycles to achieve the same outcome.

This paper presents an in-depth examination of directed flow $v_1$ of various particles produced in gold-gold, gold-lead, and lead-lead collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. The analysis is based on the LHRS and RHRS detectors' data, and incorporates a new fit parameter $\epsilon$ to account for the effects of finite geometric acceptance and event selection criteria. It also proposes a universal value of $\epsilon$ that applies equally to different collision systems. Furthermore, the research explores the link between the directed flow slope $dv_1/d\eta$ and the transverse flow parameter $p_T$.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex evolutionary problems with multiple scales, yet its high computational cost has limited its application to simple problems. To overcome this limitation, we developed a new approach by combining the ASKmethod with a sparse grid technique, making complex problems more accessible. By integrating the ASKmethod, we were able to improve the ASKmethod's ability to handle multi-dimensional problems. However, the ASKmethod still suffered from high computational costs. We introduced the sparse grid technique to reduce the computational costs associated with spatial dimensionality. We introduced the sparse grid technique, which allows us to reduce the computational costs associated with multi-dimensional problems. The new approach, known as SASKmethod, was validated through numerical examples and compared to the ASKmethod. The results showed that SASKmethod is an efficient and powerful numerical method with high accuracy and adaptability.

The Outer Complex Scaling Method has been adapted to incorporate electrostatic potentials and pave the way for calculations of finite molecules and atoms within intense direct current electric fields to arbitrary accuracy. Results have demonstrated the method's flexibility in determining adiabatic potential energy curves and minimizing lattice vibrations in molecules, all without increasing computational costs. Furthermore, this method successfully enables the accurate calculation of the critical phenomenon characteristic of molecules in DC fields, where the potential energy density decreases as it approaches its minimum value. Since the approach relies on boundary conditions instead of derivative boundary conditions, it can be effectively implemented using a variety of numerical methods. All findings with the Outer Complex Scaling Method align with those obtained through the Riemann-Liouville transformation, a quantum mechanical approach. Both methods utilize the same underlying Hamiltonian.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains widely used today for solving the Schrödinger problem within the framework of the Sinkhorn matrix scaling theory. Although the algorithm was initially proven to converge under specific positive and infinite conditions, recent research has established the presence of counterexamples. By building upon these counterexamples, this study demonstrates that even when the Schrödinger issue is undefined or has no solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm still converges. Moreover, a new method for determining whether a solution to the Schrödinger problem can be found is also presented. The results of this study provide insights into the limitations of the algorithm and can be useful in developing new applications.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to assess the top quark pair production cross-section. The measurement incorporates the entire dataset and is based on identified electrons and muons satisfying criteria mimicking a final state comprising two oppositely charged leptons, accompanied by two or more jets. Accounting for detector inefficiency, jets are reconstructed utilizing the medium template discriminant approach. The assessment yields a cross-section of 45.7 pb, in agreement with the theoretical predictions and represents 98% of the overall SM expectation.

This study investigates the unbounded movement of a particle under the influence of a force that counteracts its acceleration, originating from a fixed point. It is demonstrated that when this counteracting force is proportional to $1/r^3$, the particle undergoes unbounded movement, its acceleration consistently shifting along a circular path, ultimately leading to complex movements with a finite escape speed. Conversely, when the proportionality constant is different, specific escape velocity thresholds arise, contingent upon the initial direction and velocity of the particle. Furthermore, the asymptotic behavior of the particle's distance from the fixed point as it approaches escape velocity is extensively explored and detailed.

The correspondence between generalised Bessel functions and Janowski functions is examined, including the general form of the relationship, its consequences, and examples of functions falling within this category.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions. However, the COVID-19 pandemic significantly changed human behavior, transforming the spatial patterns of cities worldwide. In response to these changes, a predictive framework for understanding the evolution of urban activity is proposed, focusing on the interplay between individual behavior and its impact on the diversity of encounters. This approach reveals that the variations in human movement during the pandemic led to a decrease in the diversity of urban encounters compared to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, the data suggests that the alterations in human behavior, particularly a tendency to concentrate in areas with lower visitation, worsened this decline. The findings indicate that the COVID-19 pandemic had a negative effect on the diversity of urban encounters, which has the potential to influence the social and economic well-being of cities in the long term.

Researchers have been employing diverse techniques, both analytical and numerical, to tackle two-phase flow problems in irregular porous media. One such approach involves dividing mass conservation equations into individual field equations that account for liquid and gas phases. Linear and nonlinear methods for splitting these fields have unique benefits and limitations, each supported by theoretical and analytical studies. This study focuses on the nonlinear, upwind, and conservative characteristic linearization (CCL) methods for splitting pressure and saturation fields in irregular porous media. It describes a conservative cell-centered finite difference scheme for two-phase flow problems and outlines both point and finite-volume upwind schemes for splitting these fields. It also develops conservative characteristic linearization (CCL) method for splitting pressure field without relying on threshold values, leveraging irregular grid lines for accurate results. Irregular grid examples illustrate the considerable impact of irregular media characteristics on two-phase flow modeling. Nonetheless, the proposed upwind and CCL methods exhibit significant deviations from each other, highlighting potential consequences of using irregular grids in two-phase flow modeling and emphasizing the need for regular media assumptions in certain context.

The circular symmetry of an optical resonator can be broken by introducing opposing charges at its center, resulting in a preference for circular polarization. This property allows the resonator to distinguish between left- and right-handed light, effectively acting as an optical device to test the polarization of incoming light. The charge at the resonator's core can be further utilized to create specific spatial intensity patterns that vary depending on the handedness of incident light. Notably, the phenomenon observed in tableaux resonators can be applied to and demonstrated within a structured environment, such as a photonic crystal.

This note starts by reviewing the random interier polynomials, which are known to be a discrete version of the Liouville quantum superstring on a torsion-free background. We then explore the string theory's limit where the target spacetime dimension is one, leading to the derivation of Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity from a matrix model formulation. Specifically, our derivation involves the transformation of the Liouville CFT into a pair of unconstrained dual matrices, followed by taking the zero central charge limit to recover JT gravity while dismissing the conformal field theory framework.

This article delves into generalizations of the warp drive concept, primarily focusing on theoretical frameworks. One potential implementation involves creating a warp bubble through exponential space expansion, yet this approach has presented significant challenges due to the requirements for anti-gravity materials and space stabilization. Previous research mainly relied on minimal surface conditions, but this method proved insufficient to sustain warp drive propulsion. More recent developments have shown that generalized Euler-Lagrange equations can provide a more realistic framework, and our work builds upon these advancements by applying a novel approach. Using an advanced geometrical method called differential invariant-based optimization, we identify the most effective configuration for an ideal fluid warp drive with a constant scalar curvature and no external propulsion forces. Our research reveals that the most efficient configuration involves a shift from a standard to a twisted Schwarzschild geometry at the warp brake section and achieves the following key findings without using minimal surface conditions: (i) a feasible warp drive configuration with negative total mass; (ii) a method to eliminate the total mass by adjusting spacetime geometry and (iii) a possible solution to the cosmological constant problem.

As urban cities' infrastructures increase in complexity and manage substantial amounts of data, problems arise regarding data integration, interoperability, accessibility, and infrastructure maintenance. To address these challenges, a novel approach based on the fusion of sensor technologies, state-of-the-art data management, and geographic information systems has been developed to support infrastructure assessment and maintenance. This method utilizes advanced 3D modeling and network analysis to facilitate real-time data monitoring, infrastructure assessment, and maintenance planning. By implementing this approach through a user-friendly web platform, citizens can engage in various applications including reporting issues, voting, and proposing solutions for problems like traffic management, utility optimization, and urban planning. Additionally, this model enables administrators and engineers to respond efficiently and scientifically to community concerns.

Our study demonstrates how the spin of individual calcium ions within a 2D crystal responds to variations in temperature, examining both thermal manipulations and self-heating processes. Utilizing a combination of 131mCa with a long-coherent-time spin structure, we analyze the effects of temperature on the collective spin interaction and examine dephasing as a result of thermal motion, capturing both the initial dissipation process and later stages of incoherent spin behavior. We develop a model that identifies the dominant frequency of these effects, comparing it both to the expected behavior at temperature T and the rate at which neighboring ions move relative to the crystal's trapping frequency. Our analysis reveals that, on the order of a millisecond, depolarization occurs approximately three orders of magnitude faster than when the crystal is at room temperature. Additionally, our method allows for measurement of the velocity of calcium-ion motion within the crystal.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating TERS' behavior is complicated mainly because it involves intricate interactions between the tip, sample, and electromagnetic environment. Developing quantum mechanical models that consider the interplay of these components is still an emerging field. This study thoroughly examines three different quantum mechanical models describing the chemical and electromagnetic interactions involved in TERS. The models integrate density functional theory describing the sample and Semiclassical Electromagnetic Propagation and Tunneling for the tip and electromagnetic interactions. The accuracy of the models was evaluated in terms of electrical current, spatial resolution, and overall computational cost. The findings provide a framework for selecting the most suitable model for different scientific cases and serve as a foundation for further simulations and experiments in the field of TERS.

We conducted K-band (26-40 GHz) observations of 11 galaxies, including radio galaxies, quasars, and disk galaxies, using the Sardinia Radio Telescope. Our aim was to explore microwave emission in the kilohertz regime. Three sources, RC0036, RC2345, and 3C111B, exhibited significant microwave excess beyond expected synchrotron emission self-absorption, with frequencies above 30 GHz. RC0036 and RC2345 display flat-frequency spectra (betweeen 26-40 GHz), similar to gyromagnetic radiation, while 3C111B shows a double-peak structure, with one peak at 30 GHz and the other around 37 GHz. Our findings align with the hypothesis of Fast Magnetospheric Particle Transport (FMPT) proposed in past research. FMPT predicts the generation of additional emission due to the MeV cyclotron radiation of particles accelerated within source jets. If these peaks are confirmed by subsequent observations, they may serve as an irreversible marker of compact jet activity.

Although both the entropic factors associated with heat transfer in solid-state phase transitions and the extent of entropy change associated with them are crucial factors that determine a material's thermodynamic efficiency, they have not been directly quantified in relation to each other yet. This is due to the challenge of accounting for the 'lattice entropy', a component of the transition entropy that arises from phonon disorder. Using an advanced method for analyzing the movement of ionic clusters and the distribution of charge, we have directly calculated the lattice entropy for the ammonium sulfate system and found it to be significantly larger than previously estimated. Furthermore, our research indicates that the lattice entropy is correlated with the electric dipole moment of the ionic clusters and the extent of their random movement restrictions, supporting the idea that lattice entropy is a measure of disorder within the lattice structure.

In probabilistic learning, organisms adjust their behavior based on positive or
negative surprises. Some people might adopt a risk-averse strategy by changing
their behavior when expecting negative outcomes, while others might be more
sensitive to positive surprises. There's an idea that certain groups of people
might naturally have different learning strategies. We found that people who
adjusted their behavior most quickly in response to negative outcomes, while
ignoring positive ones, showed unique activity patterns in the brain and were
more likely to use a suboptimal learning rule. Importantly, this pattern wasn't
due to them making specific mistake patterns, but rather, it's a typical way of
learning for those individuals.

Focusing on the full complex versions of the $E_8$ group representation, we explore how to transform them into valid, finite-dimensional C*-algebras by imposing specific dimension constraints on the complexifications of the 7-dimensional spinors. We identify certain conditions under which the complexifications of these spinors remain non-degenerate and expressible as matrix algebras within the standard 7-dimensional complex vector space. Using this framework, we define a group called $\widetilde{E}_8$, establish the structure of its representation domain, and characterize all possible finite-dimensional linear representations. Notably, we demonstrate the existence of non-trivial, context-dependent behavior within these representations that goes beyond ordinary quantum mechanics, with theoretical implications for testing quantum contextuality using the $E_8$ group representation.

The challenge of close neighbor searching in high-dimensional time series under the Frchet distance has received significant attention. One pivotal issue in this area is the approximate close neighbor searching problem, for which current methods employ distance estimators to reduce the search space and achieve an efficient query time of O(q^2 log q / \ep^2) with q input time series. The query time remains a factor of 10 larger than the optimal known approach of brute force search. We investigated this issue by developing an algorithm utilizing the time series characters introduced in our previous work. The proposed method ensures an approximate search time of O(q / \ep^2) with q input time series, which represents an improvement by a factor of ten over the existing approach.

The inevitable inaccuracies in scientific measurements pose significant challenges and residuals from data fittings can provide valuable insights on the measurement uncertainties. However, the conventional methods to evaluate such errors rely heavily on detailed statistical information of individual measurements, which is often not the case in real-world experiments. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed various unconditional methods for unfolding measured data. Nonetheless, these existing approaches fail to fully leverage the acquired data, resulting in inaccurate calculations of background radiation and limited scope for implementing interactive algorithms. To overcome these shortcomings, our study introduces a novel, scalable, and iterative Bayesian unfolding method capable of processing large datasets in the vicinity of the true value with minimal assumptions. Furthermore, our approach can be easily adapted for various types of uncertainties and is highly compatible with detector data.

Human-robot interaction would significantly benefit from established communication protocols, especially in situations where communication breakdowns occur.  Unfortunately, such protocols have yet to be widely adopted.  As a result, humans often communicate expectations to robots in an ad-hoc manner, leading to confusion about what is expected.  To address this issue, this research investigates whether providing assistive communication can lead to a consistent understanding between humans and robots.  In a study, participants were asked to complete a task together, either with or without a supporting communication system.  The results showed that enabled or impaired communication, with the assistance of a shared autonomous system, enabled participants to develop a shared understanding of each other's intentions.  Furthermore, when the shared autonomous system communicated with humans, it accurately distinguished between its own intentions and those of the partner, highlighting its ability to navigate complex social situations.  This finding holds implications for the development of communication protocols between humans and robots, suggesting that existing knowledge can be leveraged to develop such protocols to enhance cooperative robot interactions.

For tasks such as robotics, computer vision, and geo-spatial applications, creating maps from unknown environments is a crucial necessity. Mapping techniques typically rely on techniques such as SLAM, point cloud processing, and map merging, which when combined, enable the construction of spatial awareness for robots and agents. Developing an effective mapping framework, especially in dynamic environments, requires a approach that balances detail and simplicity, particularly when using techniques such as 2D mapping, which often incorporates topology for efficient back-end processing. Despite the availability of various methods for constructing and updating 2D maps with topological structure, there is a lack of standardisation in diagram representation, particularly when it comes to navigation and decision making, which hampers the integration of different techniques and methods. In addressing this issue, a novel representation for 2D topological maps, called HiTMap, is proposed, featuring a hierarchical graph structure that mirrors the hierarchical organisation of the environment, complete with algorithms to create, update, and signalise its components. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of HiTMap in providing simple and stable representations of complex environments, which can be used as a base for decision making and navigation without requiring in-depth mapping.

Research into two-dimensional linear complementary code sets has grown in recent years due to their extensive applications. A 2-D linear code set can be viewed as a special type of multivariable function. This paper explores novel inter-group complementary code sets and 2-D Z-supplementary array code sets constructed from multivariable functions. By utilizing unitary matrices and matrices with eigenvalues, two construction methods for these code sets are developed. When the matrices used for construction have specific properties, the resulting code sets can be categorized as unitary or Z-supplementary array code sets. A variety of inter-group complementary code sets are presented, along with some ideal properties of two-dimensional linear code sets, such as two-dimensional unitary, Z-supplementary array, complete complementarity, and two-dimensional complete complementarity.

We present an innovative low-dose X-ray computed tomography (CT) image reconstruction technique that utilizes multiple energy levels (PECT) to distinguish and separate various materials based on their known X-ray attenuation properties and inherent noise. Our method incorporates an alternative to traditional optimization methods by transforming the complex, non-convex PECT problem into an improved form. Our algorithm relies on iterative calculations involving three key processes: (1) using calibrated X-ray energy projections for CT image reconstruction via advanced statistical methods; (2) identifying noise patterns and factors affecting sensor readings using a complex statistical model; (3) using a cutting-edge material decomposition algorithm to separate and distinguish various materials based on X-ray attenuation values, given their characteristic curves. Our method effectively deters the influence of noise and inaccurate estimates by introducing a degree of flexibility into our framework. Our results from multiple experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique in extracting CT images from few, noisy X-ray measurements; accurately detecting various materials; and identifying patterns, such as materials behind each other, in multiple material scenarios.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which doesn't account for electron spillover and nonlocal behavior predicts the same light behavior as the more accurate hydrodynamic model with electron spillover, but a quantum hydrodynamics model which excludes electron spillover produces significantly contrasting results. Furthermore, we reveal that the frequency dependence in metal behavior predicted by the more accurate hydrodynamic model, which considers electron spillover, converges towards a quantum hydrodynamics model which doesn't account for electron spillover at very small gaps.

The task of Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER) involves selecting the most suitable entities from a database to complete a query based on the context provided. Current approaches to CNER are limited in that they solely assess the context and target entity without considering how relevant the retrieved entities are to the target entity. This paper investigates the effectiveness of a metric called Term Relevance Response (TRR) in improving CNER performance by combining the context and target entity to create diverse retrieval queries. Our experiments using two datasets reveal that TRR significantly enhances state-of-the-art CNER models by 10.7-15.1% MRR improvement and 6.2-12.5% Masked Label Matching accuracy.

For users employed in fields such as healthcare and fitness, understanding variations in long-term data over extensive periods is crucial, yet presenting these changes can be extremely challenging due to the high number of multivariate data points and uneven sampling intervals. Existing time-series visualization techniques primarily focus on a narrow time frame, typically no more than a month, and often struggle with stations that have high numbers of missing data or irregular sampling patterns, thereby limiting the analysis to just a fraction of available data. This paper introduces TeraTime, a new visualization system designed specifically to help users understand and analyze large amounts of data spanning extended periods and irregularly sampled time frames. TeraTime facilitates deep analysis by enabling users to explore self-identified patterns over both contractable and expandable time frames. By combining an interactive timescale with relevant context, TeraTime allows users to gain a more in-depth understanding of patterns, both large and small. Through evaluations involving actual users analyzing data, as well as as surveys and interviews, we have confirmed TeraTime's engagement capabilities and gathered valuable insights to inform future research.

We introduced an novel node-level graph neural network (GNN) called the Heterogeneous Resemblance Graph Neural Network (HRGNN), which captures connections between nodes through shared subgraphs before applying GNNs for classification tasks. We extracted patient similarities from subgraphs and demonstrated better performance than traditional approaches like k-nearest neighbors on real-world electronic health records (EHRs). Additionally, our method was tested on a misclassified node and showed the potential to identify uncoded or missing information in EHRs. Experimental results on two real-world datasets revealed that HRGNN surpasses the current state-of-the-art in multi-node graph classification by 2.0-6.9% in precision and 3.2-22.1% in F1-score.

Within the framework of Debye-Hückel theory, an electrostatic analysis is performed to examine the influence of solvent polarization on the electric double layer formed at a soft charged surface. The hydrodynamic properties of the polymer brush are computed using the lubrication approximation within mean-field theory. The solvent polarization effects are accounted for through a parameter derived from Penning-Purcell effect considerations, applicable to stiff brushes. The solvent density is found to fluctuate at the surface, generating a discontinuity in the electric field according to Maxwell's equations. These equations also reveal that the polarization of the solvent leads to an apparent decrease in the charge of the surface, thus modifying the electric field near the surface and the ion distribution. As a result, the solvent polarization gives rise to a decrease in the adsorbed layer thickness of ions $\lambda_{\mp}$ and the surface charge density of the electrolyte $\sigma_{\mp}$. The relationship between the solvent polarization, surface charge, and ion adsorption is analyzed, showing that the solvent polarization generates an induced charge density that is governed by the surface charge density. Furthermore, the solvent polarization is found to produce a shift in the phase transition of the brush towards lower surface charge densities. The computation of the stiffness per ion $\alpha$ reveals that the stiffness is reduced by the solvent polarization, resulting in an increase of the brush volume. The computation of the compressibility $Q_{2}$ shows that the solvent polarization modifies the mechanical properties of the brush. The

The growing reliance on software in our lives highlights the necessity for advanced methods of extracting and understanding specifications to facilitate seamless communication between developers and end users. To address this need, this research presents a two-stage framework for automating specification extraction from non-formatted text. Our approach combines the use of Natural Language Processing and machine learning techniques, ultimately allowing for the transformation of unstructured specifications into a modified Business Rule Definition Grammar format. To demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of our methodology, we conducted a study involving 132 specifications from a leading software repository. By testing various feature combinations and models, we achieved optimal results with an accuracy rate of 88.7% on the entire dataset and 91.7% on a subset of 43 specifications defined by IDEF0.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-node, multi-carrier wireless network that uses network coding with independent data transmission from each source to its destinations through a common relay. We evaluate the static and dynamic scheduling methods within a single time slot and our results show that a dynamic schedule can achieve significant gains in energy efficiency, surpassing the static schedule by up to 100%. By further optimizing the relay's transmission power using our proposed algorithm, we found that a submodular property exists which enables an efficient solution through a greedy algorithm. We found that our method outperforms a comparative energy-efficient approach used in recent studies by an average improvement of 20-50%. We were also able to determine the optimal energy-efficient schedule with the highest energy gain, which corresponds to the relay using its full transmission capacity in a simultaneous multi-cast schedule. We verified the effectiveness of our method using simulations conducted on diverse networks, which reaffirmed its ability to achieve substantial energy gains compared to a static schedule. Moreover, the results showed that as the number of active sources in the network increases, our method leads to higher energy efficiency without compromising throughput.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific information includes details on the energy spacing between impurity states, direct and indirect coupling strengths among these impurities, and their collective excitations. Utilizing sophisticated calculation methods and an advanced model of electron behavior, the researchers analyzed a particular scenario in which manganese atoms form clusters on a superconducting material surface. Their analysis demonstrates that the resulting cluster impurities exhibit distinct and isolated energy states, facilitating the development of a novel and efficient spin transfer mechanism between these clusters and the surrounding material surface. This transfer mechanism is particularly significant in a specific quantum energy state, known as the Yu--Shiba--Rusinon (YSR) state, as it can be easily manipulated through changes in the cluster's magnetic properties. Additionally, the researchers observed an unusual indirect spin transfer process between the cluster impurities, which is enabled by the collective excitations of the YSR states. This indirect spin transfer mechanism is challenging to study in experiments due to its relatively weak contribution compared to other competing processes. As this mechanism is more significant in smaller clusters, the researchers anticipate an increased likelihood of observing this phenomenon in experiments involving cluster manipulation techniques.

The NA62 experiment at CERN's proton beam facility has published its initial research on the K+/pi+ nu nu decay search. Based on data collected in 2016 with an accumulated dataset of 0.5 x 10^12 collected events, the research set a sensitivity limit of 6 x 10^-10, supplementing a past study by the K2K collaboration with a limit of 6.6 x 10^-7, thereby reducing the uncertainty by a factor of 10^5. Utilizing the decay-in-motion technique, the research identified pion nuclei moving at high speed, thereby providing superior sensitivity relative to stationary pion studies. The research employed a novel technique where X-ray emitting carbon nuclei within the beam interacted with photons from K+ decay, producing emissions detectable by the Extrapace X-ray detector. A total of 1245 K+ decay events were identified with a background of 3637, thereby resulting in a frequency limit of K+ decay with 3.04 sigma's statistical significance.

This research introduces a robust approach to bias reduction in distribution-to-distribution scan matching, incorporating a Dynamic Neural Network Filter (DNF) to correct path navigation. Following the initial state estimation and map alignment of an optimized state transition model, the proposed method involves embedding DNF within a dynamic state filter to modulate navigation states. By leveraging an artificial feature design, a navigation optimizer can be formed to exploit the inherent structure of optimization problems, improving the performance of dynamic state filters. Consequently, this method achieves accelerated convergence and enhanced robustness, achieving errors under 0.2m in both indoor and outdoor settings, while also demonstrating minimal computational overhead, approximately 10% that of a standard EKF at 20Hz.

Recent advancements in machine learning have led to the development of complex, high-performance algorithms for processing visual data. Despite this, deep learning-based algorithms require a substantial amount of memory and time, limiting their use in applications of of visual processing, such as search engines for images, video surveillance systems, and satellite image analysis systems. A new approach aims to overcome these limitations by leveraging the computational capabilities of GPU and CPU on a single device, using a combination of Sobel operators for edge detection in pixel values. According to our tests, this simple method can effectively compare to deep learning-based algorithms based on Brute Force metrics.

Using the framework of an iterative rate model of electron groups, we investigate the non-linear high-fluence XANES (near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure) spectrum of the 1s $\rightarrow$ 3p transition in the neon atom. This model commences with a fundamental rate equation describing the initial detachment of an electron from the initial ground state. Each subsequent step involves the transfer of this electron between the 1s, 2s, 2p, and 3s, 3p orbitals prior to its final transition to a 3p continuum. Each orbital's density is calculated via the Hartree-Fock-Slater model. This multi-electron scenario is subsequently combined with the spin-polarized framework of the $X^{2}B$ M\,4 edge model developed by Choudhury and Sen (2017). Applying the rate equation to each electron subgroup, we derive individual spectral contributions, which are subsequently summed to produce the overall spin-polarised spectrum. This rate equation method, however, introduces a novel means of explaining the observed spin-polarisation patterns in the neon gas target, which ultimately results in the production of circularly polarised radiation. This latter effect is found to be directly linked to the asymmetrical shape of the 3p valence orbitals, which exhibits distinct forward and rear regions. This phenomenon is identified as the primary factor responsible for the observed non-linear, high-fluence XANES spectral response

The application of Deep Learning (DL) has significantly contributed to the advancement of Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) systems. Nonetheless, such systems are vulnerable to malicious attacks that generate counterfeit input data, rendering DL-based classification results inaccurate. To overcome this challenge, this research presents a novel approach that combines two opposing neural networks - one generating authentic signals and the other creating adversarial signals - to develop a resilient and universal AMC system against adversarial attacks. The proposed architecture, referred to as the 'Blend GAN' framework, is tested and verified to provide superior performance in classification procedures, as evidenced by an increased signal-to-noise ratio and superior error rates when compared to conventional methods.

Identifying multiple sclerosis (MS) lesions accurately is vital for disease monitoring and treatment decision-making. Creating a universal segmentation model is challenging due to limited training data and dataset-specific characteristics. In this study, we analyzed how to continuously learn from new, unlabelled dataset additions while also comparing the performance to training a model from scratch with the newly acquired data. We found that integrating unlabelled images can be beneficial, but it's essential to carefully assess the reliability of each image to avoid compromising model performance. To achieve this, we utilized a two-stream neural network approach that simultaneously employs supervised and unsupervised learning streams. We evaluated our method on a combined dataset of 110 patients from two hospitals and demonstrated that continuous learning can be effective in medical image segmentation tasks. Our findings also highlight the importance of selecting reliable images for domain adaptation and the challenges associated with it.

The 2022 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing, held in Budapest, Hungary, features a competition focusing on image representation and understanding through the analysis of contrast, with the goal of advancing machine learning methods for discovering and quantifying visual patterns. This work details our entry, which tackles the task of contrast contrastive learning, where images are categorized based on their visual properties instead of their semantic meanings. We propose a framework where training data is divided into two groups: one containing synthesised images that highlight specific visual attributes, and the other consisting of regular images without these attributes. Our approach relies on a dual-headed model where one head processes regular images, and the other processes synthesised images, both aiming to distinguish between the two groups. This setup where synthesised images make it harder for the model to identify regular images, mimics the idea of contrast contrastive learning. Our experiment on the ImageNet dataset shows that our two-head training strategy enhances image classification accuracy. When transferred to other tasks, our model with non-identical two-head training yields a significant improvement in their performance.

When learning a dynamical system through data, inaccuracies in modeling can hinder the performance of machine learning algorithms, causing them to produce subpar predictions. In contrast to existing approaches that focus on predicting system behavior, our study centers on identifying the source of errors. By formulating a dynamic framework based on Markov processes, we develop both universal and conditional measures to evaluate model inaccuracies, quantifying their impact on predicting system states. These methods can be applied to any model having a probabilistic form that we treat as a Markov source. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply it to the prediction of chaotic systems, specifically predicting data from the Lorenz system, even in the presence of noise. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the relationship between model inaccuracies and the requirements for accurate predictions.

The formation of massive stars and runaway stars is often linked to the development of infrared dark clouds (IRDCs), which represent the most advanced stage of star formation. Through the examination of spectral line data from the CCAT-TeV telescope at an 11-240 km/s l velocity, our research confirms the existence of a primordial star-forming region within the Dragon IRDC at 440 pc from the Sun. At this location, our findings indicate the expansion of a central core with a mass between 30 and 70 solar masses. Additionally, we have identified highly rotating, sub-interstellar column densities of gas surrounding the core, amounting to 30 solar masses, which exhibits signs of shock through balanced gas and outflow measurements. If developed properly, this core has the potential to give rise to a massive star. If it becomes disrupted, its material could contribute to the formation of additional low-mass stars within adjacent molecular clouds."

A novel computational model, PopSyCLE, is employed to estimate the formation of Primordial Black Holes as a form of Dark Matter within a given mass range. PopSyCLE takes into account key factors influencing Black Hole creation, including a variable inflationary scenario and multiple possibilities for scale factor multiplication during e-fold calculations. We use the PopSyCLE model to analyze a variety of theoretical scenarios and calculate the percentage of Dark Matter comprised by Primordial Black Holes, examining the interplay between this phenomenon and the expected Densities derived from the Cosmic Microwave Background data. Additionally, cross-referencing these findings with constraints imposed by gravitational lensing observations further refines our understanding of PBH DM.

We conducted research into systems consisting of homogeneous wedges made up of spheres, where the wedge angles varied from 360 to 1080 degrees. Unlike traditional molecular models, these units exhibit unique geometry that may resemble the structure of nanomaterials and certain biomolecules. In simulations with high density configurations of these units, we observed phases characterized by modulation in the direction of nematic order and isolated units. These modulations significantly impacted the mechanical properties of the material. Conversely, phases characterized by random arrangement of the units displayed two-dimensional ordering similar to systems consisting of cylindrical particles. In high density configurations, these random arrangements transformed into ordered structures resembling a honeycomb pattern. In low density configurations, these random arrangements transformed into ordered structures consisting of large, curved domains. In both high and low density configurations, these random arrangements maintained their mechanical properties, which resulted in their resistance to cracking under tension.

The widespread use of pre-trained language models in multiple downstream tasks has created a need for more efficient fine-tuning methods to reduce costs and accelerate development processes.  We investigate fine-tuning strategies for classification tasks and propose an innovative approach, incorporating special tokens to adjust the position of attention distributions and adapt to task-specific data.  Experimental results on the Google Dataset Catalog and multiple NLP NLP tasks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing strategies, with improved performance that is both more efficient and faster to train.

A key challenge in multi-object optimization lies in addressing preferences that are interdependent and non-comparable. This issue is particularly prominent in the context of a set addition problem where one needs to determine the optimal additional features or attributes to include. Most existing approaches rely on a non-contextual evaluation of preferences by individually considering each feature's contribution. By contrast, a contextual evaluation takes into consideration the interactions between features, thus providing more accurate evaluations. However, contextual evaluations are often impractical to be implemented due to their high computational demands. This study proposes a novel context-aware preference learning model that can efficiently handle a set addition problem. Through theoretical analysis, it is proven that our model can effectively learn both contextual and non-contextual preferences. Experimental results reveal that our model can learn both types of preferences more accurately and efficiently than state-of-the-art approaches. This research has been successfully validated on a variety of real-world datasets. Furthermore, our model performs well even with incomplete data and requires minimal computational resources. Overall, this study offers a comprehensive exploration of both contextual and non-contextual preference learning, a crucial aspect of mathematical programming that has been long overlooked.

Our investigation explores thermodynamic properties in glass-forming polymer fluids through equilibrium simulations with fluctuation dissipation theory. We discovered that dynamic properties are heavily influenced by thermodynamic parameters but retain memory of past conditions. The intensity of this historical influence and the time frame associated with it can be decoupled and better understood using correlation functions and proportionality constants. The proportionality constants are found to adapt to changing thermodynamic states while conforming to time-dependent rules. Furthermore, applying the hierarchy of non-equilibrium dynamics and the aging phenomenon to these constants reveals a coherent mathematical framework, which also applies to the relaxation times of structural and dynamic quantities. This set of rules may be referred to as the thermodynamic-dynamic hierarchy.

Our investigation into how language models process rejection during development yields
some unexpected findings that challenge our initial theory. Specifically, we created
a series of examples leading up to a sentence to test model rejection of
ungrammatical words, but a notable exception arose in our experiments with
transformer-based language models. Despite initial indications of successful
rejection, models actually select preferred words based on context, it appears that
language models do not effectively process 'no such word' by a certain stage of
processing, instead choosing between candidate words. We examine the logical
consequences of models making inference predictions before evaluating the word
existence. Furthermore, we investigate if models are actually inconsistent in their
judgments or if this exception arises from the data itself, discovering that in
human evaluations word existence does have clear implications. Our findings also
show that boosting transformer performance through masked language learning actually
increases, rather than decreasing, the error rate for rejecting non-existent
words. Our code and data for these experiments can be found at
https://github.com/google-research-datasets/reject/.

To improve Decoding orientations in Neural Machine Translation, this research introduces a novel mechanism called the Look-ahead Focus target, which enables the model to focus on both short-term and long-term comprehension of the translation by assessing the relevance of generated tokens in advance. Unlike conventional methods relying on attention or salience maps, this approach targets an enhanced focus on translation quality and is adaptable to existing state-of-the-art NMT models. The proposed mechanism exhibits substantial performance enhancements on various translation tasks and is particularly notable in producing more concise translations while maintaining or enhancing their level of accuracy.

This passage uses a generalized version of the Kontsevich formalism to determine the weights of the connection and curvature graphs within the context of a derived symplectic algebra. It structures the calculation in a manner that is adaptable to other Poisson structures. The study demonstrates that a key structural element in this framework is a trilinear form derived from the multiplicative 3-pre-Lie derivative of the structure's homotopy. This form serves as the foundation for a connection on the structure's derived symmetric bimodule, enabling the calculation of graphs. Specifically, weights for graphs involving two vertices can be computed via iterative applications of the trilinear form, while the addition of vertices requires the integration of this form over corresponding graph bases. In cases where the structure's homotopy derives from a quantized simplicial complex, this approach leads to a geometrically natural interpretation. Furthermore, a secondary result describes a related form for general graph weights.

This research involves determining the causal dynamics of two large-N interacting scalar fields in a CFT-like system at high temperature, which is relevant to the study of the Dirac-Bergman system. We make use of a high temperature expansion to derive precise expressions for the causal dynamics. It's found that when the coupling constant exceeds a specific threshold, thermal equilibrium information becomes inaccessible to the causal dynamics, whereas smaller coupling values do not impede causal convergence. Notably, this investigation reveals that thermal properties cause persistent information loss throughout the causal dynamics. This phenomenon is reminiscent of the causal stored information property that governs CFTs interacting with vacuums.

This paper serves as a complement to a previous work published in 2018, which proposed the Path-Condensation Method for pricing Asian options using conditional expectations of path functions with respect to a Markov process. The current paper aims to simplify the previously developed Method in two key ways. Firstly, the new approach eliminates the requirement for independent and identically distributed path sets, which can lead to computational inefficiencies. Secondly, the Method can be applied even when the Markov transition function cannot be readily accessed. To achieve this, the framework is revised by replacing the Markov process with a more broad class of deterministic spatially homogeneous random fields on compact intervals. It is shown that this revised framework captures a broad range of pricing schemes, including the Path-Condensation Method, the Path-Expectation Framework, Quasi-Green's Function (QGF) formula, and the Feynman-Kac formula.

The identity of the gamma-ray "Horns" remains a mystery, dominating the sky at energies above 100 GeV and below 10 GeV, and distinguishing themselves from lower energy data by lacking a peak at 100 GeV. One potential explanation for these gamma-ray features is dispersed radiation from galaxy clusters, broken up into smaller energy segments by CMB photons. Our 3D model of the galaxy cluster universe predicts that this scattered gamma-ray signal should peak around 10 GeV and account for up to 25% of the global gamma-ray flux at higher energies, and our simulation shows that such a scenario can fit observed data, and it's likely that future telescopes will be able to verify this theory by identifying specific spatial patterns in the gamma-ray signal.

Early universe events involving massive particles, beyond the scope of the Standard Model, may release distinctive cosmic microwave background signatures as a signature of new physics, both with and without primordial features. Determining the characteristics of these features, however, proves challenging due to their intricate mathematical nature. On the other hand, events involving the collision of two heavy particles, one of which is part of a dark sector doublet, could potentially create distinctive features in the primordial primordial power spectrum, regardless of the mass scale of new physics involved. A simple fact explains this: the lightest particle in such a sector, often referred to as pristine, remains relatively light and can easily decay into particles beyond the Standard Model, resulting in features, as observed. Furthermore, the phenomenon is not solely dependent on the mass scale of new physics involved, as demonstrated by comparisons between the relativistic and non-relativistic limits. A distinctive feature, as predicted by the cosmological collider physics principle, is unlikely to be affected by future observations aimed at validating the standard primordial primordial power spectrum.

Understanding how visual recognition models work is essential, and to achieve this, researchers typically rely on explanations from the knowledge gained by training these models on large datasets. However, conventional methods for explaining artificial neural networks confound visual and semantic aspects, making it difficult to gain insight into which specific aspects of an image are influencing the model's output. In response, we introduce the Latent Visual-Semantic Filter Focus approach, which uses a specially designed network to separate the visual and semantic components of an image, and then uses this separation to discover which parts of an image are capturing attention from the model. Our approach is unique because it decouples the visual and semantic aspects, and passes these components through a filter to discover which specific features are being focused by the model. We test the Latent Visual-Semic Filter Focus approach on the ImageNet dataset and find that it facilitates easier analysis and understanding of the model's internal workings.

The superconducting pairing in cuprates remains a mystery, with many theories being explored but none providing a conclusive solution. The unique properties of cuprates, such as robustness to disorder and complex magnetic interactions, set them apart from other high-temperature superconductors, creating difficulties in modeling their behavior. To address this issue, a simple one-dimensional model with dimerized Cu-O bonds is examined, with the possibility of coupled dimer formation being regulated by an adjustable parameter. This allows for the modeling of different coupling regimes and the investigation of attractive interactions between dimerized sites. Our findings demonstrate that long-range attractive interactions can occur at any distance in Cu-O coupling configurations, with the presence of magnetic monopolarons not necessarily requiring short-range coupling. Furthermore, our results show that high temperatures can facilitate long-range coupling and the formation of singlet bonds. The high temperature stability of singlet bonds, coupled with their resistance to disorder and the absence of pseudogap states, makes them an attractive model for the pairing mechanism in cuprates. The application of quantum fluctuations enhances the Cooper-pairing mechanism and the formation of bound states, with the phenomenon of rung-singlet exciton, arising due to a competitive interaction, potentially contributing to the observed zero-energy bound state at the Fermi level.

Nonrandomly sampled datasets present a specific challenge to traditional statistical analysis, primarily due to the introduction of hidden variables that skew initial conclusions. Causal structural discovery methods can overcome this limitation, aligning with the principles of directed acyclic graphs. This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods on real-world data derived from the Michigan Pandemic Study. This multi-wave study investigates the causes and risk factors of the pandemic in an individual perspective. Causal structural discovery output from this dataset includes merged structural models, marginal independence graphs, shaded graphs, hidden variable graphs, causal graphs, Markov equivalent classes, and causal Markov equivalent classes. A novel approach is presented to streamline model selection and integration processes from existing literature.
